chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
Buying a property as a couple is a wonderful milestone — and an important legal decision. Especially for common-law partners, whose rights differ from those of married couples, it's essential to structure the purchase properly to protect yourselves.

This guide covers the ways of holding property as a couple, the importance of an agreement, and the protections to put in place.

Informational content, not legal advice: consult a notary. Each chapter ends with a lined “My Notes” page.

chapters.title: Married vs. Common-Law Partners
chapters.html:
Understanding why status changes everything.

In Quebec, married or civil-union couples benefit from protective rules (the family patrimony) that govern the family residence. Common-law partners, however, do NOT have these automatic protections: in the event of separation or death, their rights depend mainly on what is written down (title, agreement, will).

Many common-law partners are unaware of this reality and end up with nothing. The good news: you can protect yourself with the right documents.

Emilie's tip

If you're common-law partners, don't assume you're protected “like married couples”: you're not, automatically. What you put in writing makes all the difference.

chapters.title: How to Hold the Property
chapters.html:
Choosing the ownership structure.

  • In undivided ownership, in equal shares (50/50) or according to each person's contribution.
  • The title of ownership must clearly reflect who owns what.
  • If only one partner is on the title, the other may end up with no right to the property, even after years and payments.

How the property is registered on the title is a defining decision: make it with full knowledge, with the notary.

Emilie's tip

Make sure the title truly reflects your agreement. If one of you contributes more to the down payment, say so and document it: memory and love don't hold up in court.

chapters.title: The Agreement Between Partners
chapters.objective: Planning for the unexpected in writing.
chapters.html:
Planning for the unexpected in writing.

An agreement (often called an indivision agreement or a cohabitation agreement) sets out in advance: the division of shares, who pays what (mortgage, taxes, upkeep), what happens in the event of separation (buyout, sale, timelines) and in the event of death (together with the will).

It's a bit like insurance: you hope never to use it, but it avoids painful conflicts if life changes.

Emilie's tip

Draw up an agreement BEFORE buying, while all is well. Writing it calmly together is infinitely easier than negotiating in the pain of a separation.

chapters.title: Action Plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, in concrete terms.

This week

  1. Clarify our status and our actual protections.
  2. Decide on the division of shares.

Within 30 days

  1. Have an agreement drafted by a notary.
  2. Update our wills accordingly.

After that

  1. Register the property on the title in line with our agreement.

chapters.title: Resources & Glossary
chapters.html:
• Family patrimony: protections for married / civil-union couples.
  • Common-law partners: without automatic protections; the written record prevails.
  • Undivided ownership: ownership by several people, in equal shares or by contribution.
  • Indivision agreement: the arrangement governing shares, payments, and exits.
  • Title of ownership: must reflect the couple's actual agreement.
